sections.h2: Where and how to file a deed in Mio
sections.html:
Oscoda County has one office for both the Clerk and the Register of Deeds. It works out of the Government Administration Building at 311 South Morenci Avenue in downtown Mio, MI 48647. Phone 989-826-1110, fax 989-826-1136, or email countyclerk@oscodacountymi.com. Mailed items go to PO Box 399.

Doors are open on weekdays from half past eight until half past four, with a break at noon for an hour, and the office shuts on most federal holidays. Walk-ins are fine. Documents arrive in three ways:

  • Over the counter in Mio.
  • By regular mail to the box, with a stamped return envelope so the original comes home.
  • By courier, UPS or FedEx, to the street address.

Title agents based elsewhere can send files through CSC Ingeo, EPN (E-Recording Partners) or Simplifile. Certified court documents and death certificates cannot go that route, so ask first.

The numbers below come from the state schedule in MCL 600.2567. Phone 989-826-1110 for the exact total, including any card or vendor surcharge, before a check goes in the mail.

Recording fees for Oscoda County documents
ServiceFee
Entering and recording a document of any length$30.00
Each added instrument released or assigned by the same paper$3.00
Copy of a record$1.00 a page
Certifying a recorded paper$5.00
Name search by staff50 cents a year, $5.00 minimum

Copies are handed out on paper only, and phone photos of records are not allowed.

sections.h2: Transfer tax on a Mio-area sale
sections.html:
Two taxes ride on every deed. The state charges $3.75 per $500 of price (MCL 207.525), and the county charges 55 cents per $500 (MCL 207.504). A part-block rounds up. The price must be shown on the deed itself or in an attached affidavit.

Exemptions the two laws share, and one they do not:

  • Price under $100.
  • Transfers ordered by a court with no price attached.
  • Boundary straightening with no money paid.
  • Quitclaims that only repair a flaw in title already held.
  • Family deeds from parent to child or grandchild, which excuse the state tax and nothing more.

Put the exemption in writing on the deed. The seller is normally the party who bears the tax, so ask your closing agent to show it as a line on your side of the settlement statement.

Anything from 1985 forward is electronic, and older material is on microfiche. New filings show up online within five days. Each one is time stamped, checked, numbered, indexed and scanned.

All real estate records are public, and anyone may search them in the office or online. Searches go by the property owner's name, and several public computers sit in the office. Staff do not run title searches. They send people to a title company or a private searcher. Ownership follows whatever documents the office has recorded, so a seller holding an old unrecorded deed should file it before listing.

Online tools come in three kinds. Fidlar Laredo is a subscription program with a software download, popular for heavy searching. Fidlar Tapestry bills as you go and spans several Michigan counties. A free direct search link also exists on the county page.

Title fraud is a real risk on vacant and seasonal property, where nobody sees the mail. Alerts are worth setting up before you list, and again after closing if you keep other land in the county.

Property Fraud Alert costs county landowners nothing and starts at 1-800-728-3858 or propertyfraudalert.com/mioscoda. It alerts you right away when a paper is recorded against your parcel. The Youngblood Law, House Bills 5598 and 5599, signed in November 2024, makes filing a fraudulent document with any Michigan register of deeds a felony.

sections.h2: What a deed must show before Mio accepts it
sections.html:
The office drafts nothing and keeps no legal forms. Staff recommend an attorney or title company, and for do-it-yourselfers they name MichiganLegalHelp.org and eforms.com as starting places. They cannot say how a deed should be prepared.

MCL 565.201 governs the page itself: dark ink signatures with printed names, the grantee's address, the drafter's name and address, and a 2.5 inch clear top margin on the first page. MCL 211.135 governs tax proof. Before a warranty deed records, the county treasurer certifies that no liens or tax titles are held and that five years of taxes are paid. A quitclaim without warranty covenants is excused. Get the certificate from the Oscoda County Treasurer and carry it with the deed to Mio.

sections.h2: Selling a house in Oscoda County
sections.html:
Oscoda County is the only county in Michigan with no incorporated city or village, so the county offices in Mio are the nearest local government for every parcel. Mio, the seat, sits in the Au Sable River valley where M-33 and M-72 meet, and the south half of the county lies in the Huron National Forest.

The population is estimated at 8,723, up 6.1% from the 2020 count of 8,219. The middle home value is $125,500, owner occupancy is 87.2%, and monthly rent is $681. Housing units total 7,792 against 3,788 households, which shows how many homes sit empty or are used seasonally. Only 24 building permits were issued in 2025. If you are selling a seasonal cabin, expect a buyer pool of out-of-area owners, and confirm internet service at the address for remote-work buyers.

Before listing a cabin or woodland home, search the owner's name at the register and ask the county treasurer for the tax certificate, since both steps affect closing speed.

sections.h2: Closing steps for a cabin or home sale
sections.html:
A sale here follows a short, predictable path. The title company or your attorney prepares the deed, and the register only records it.

  1. Search the owner's name at the register to confirm every earlier deed is recorded.
  2. Request the treasurer's certificate if the deed carries warranty covenants.
  3. Put the price on the deed or attach the affidavit, and write any transfer tax exemption on the face of the deed.
  4. Send the original by mail, courier, e-recording or hand delivery, with the recording fee.
  5. Enroll in Property Fraud Alert so a later filing against your parcel reaches you.

A cash buyer needs the same recording and pays the same fees. The savings come from skipping lender approval and appraisal, not from skipping any county step. Keep the recorded original or a copy of it with your closing papers. Call 989-826-1110 if you are unsure which of these applies to a family transfer.

faqs.q: Where is the Oscoda County register's office?
faqs.a: It is at 311 South Morenci Avenue in Mio, MI 48647. Letters go to PO Box 399, and the main number is 989-826-1110.

faqs.q: Does Oscoda County take deeds by mail?
faqs.a: Yes. Send the original to the PO Box, or ship by UPS or FedEx to the street address, and include a self-addressed stamped envelope for the return.

faqs.q: Which e-recording vendors does Oscoda County use?
faqs.a: CSC Ingeo, EPN and Simplifile. Certified court documents and death certificates are excluded, so call before sending one.

faqs.q: How is transfer tax figured on an Oscoda County sale?
faqs.a: The state charges $3.75 and the county charges 55 cents for every $500 of price, if no exemption fits. A partial $500 block counts as a full one, so a price just over a block boundary adds to the bill.

faqs.q: Does the Mio office search titles?
faqs.a: No. It is a recording office and refers people to title companies or private searchers, though you may search names yourself in the office or online.
